The house resumed from Thursday, June 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of Bill No. 253, to make provision with respect to forces of the United States of America when visiting Canada and with respect to the exercise of discipline and to the internal administration of such forces, and of the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Probe.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the motion for second reading of this bill and the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City, that the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter
be referred to the committee on external affairs, have occasioned a debate that has covered a wide range of international politics.
I shall not venture to take the time of the house to comment on many things which have been said in the course of that debate and with which most members of the house would be in agreement, or upon a number of things that have been said with which I cannot agree but which I do not think it is necessary to point out specifically. There are some points, however, upon which I feel it is my duty to give accurate and precise information to the house before it is called upon to vote on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City.
The first point with which I wish to deal is the effect of that kind of motion. There seems to be some uncertainty as to the effect of an amendment to a motion that a 'bill be read a second time, referring the subject matter of that bill to a committee for consideration. I have discussed this matter with the Clerk, whose experience in things of this kind is, as everyone knows, wide and broad. I have also looked at some of the authorities and I venture to suggest that this is the situation. When a motion for the second reading of a bill has been put a member may move that the bill be not now read a second time but that its subject matter be referred to either a standing or a special committee. If the amendment carries the bill is killed for the time being. There is always the rule that when the house decides that a bill be not now read a second time the door remains open for a motion to place, it on the order paper for second leading at another time. But if the amendment that the bill be not now read a second time carries and the subject matter be referred to a committee, a motion to place the bill on the order paper for second reading cannot be made so long as the subject matter is before the committee. The subject matter cannot be dealt with in the house while it is under reference to the committee. If the committee reports recommending the passage of legislation identical in terms to the bill the subject matter of which was referred to the committee a motion for the second reading could be made without having the bill previously read again a first time. But if the committee does not so report or does not report at all the bill cannot be dealt with in the house. If the report of the committe is not for the introduction of legislation identical in terms with the bill, and the report is concurred in, that is the end of the matter. So that, in fact, as a matter of practical application, there is little chance for a bill, the subject matter of which has been referred to a

The second point with which I wish to deal is the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) with respect to the effect of legislation or proposed legislation recently submitted by the President to the Congress of the United States. I think it is necessary that the Canadian public know what the situation is and not be left under the impression that might have been gathered from newspaper dispatches which have had to be qualified previously in statements to the house but which, unfortunately, the hon. member chose to put on the record last night.
There was recommended by the President to the Congress of the United States on May 26 a bill to replace the act which had been passed in 1940, and which was an act to authorize the secretaries of war and navy to assist the governments of the American republics to increase their military and naval establishments. The President, in submitting this bill, said, among other things:
As stated in my message to the 79th congress our army and navy have maintained cordial relations of collaboration with the armed forces of other American republics, within the framework of the good-neighbour policy. Under authorization of the congress, military and naval training missions have been sent to various American republics.
And further down, he said:
The American republics have assumed new responsibilities for their mutual defence and for the maintenance of peace in the act of Chapul-tepec and the charter of the united nations.
Hon. members know that the act of Chapultepec is an act adopted by the members of the Pan-American union to which Canada does not belong. I continue:
The close collaboration of the American republics provided for in the act of Chapultepec, the proposed treaty to be based upon that act, and other basic inter-American documents, make it highly desirable to standardize military organization, training methods, and equipment as has been recommended by the inter-American defence board.
Canada is not a member of the interAmerican defence board, which is an organism of the Pan-American union. I continue:
Under the bill transmitted herewith, the army and navy, acting in conjunction with the Department of State, would be permitted to continue in the future a general programme of collaboration with the armed forces of our sister republics with a view to facilitating the adoption of similar technical standards.
That is the proposed legislation submitted to the United States congress by the President. In submitting it, he had this to say:
[Mr. St. Laurent.}
The collaboration authorized by the bill could be extended also to Canada whose cooperation with the United States in matters affecting their common defence is of particular importance.
That being the situation, it was stated here the other day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this legislation had no effect whatsoever on the arrangements outlined and described by him in his statement to the house on February 12, 1947. I think it is only fair that the Canadian public should realize that such is the situation, and that this legislation was legislation to replace the act to which I have referred, an act authorizing the secretaries of war and of navy to assist the governments of the American republics to increase their military and naval establishments and for other purposes. The legislation relates exclusively to the projects arising out of the arrangements of the act of Chapultepec and to implement the undertakings made by those who are parties to that act. It is something which could be extended to Canada, which could be extended to any other nation, which could be extended even to Russia, but it would have to be by arrangement with the sovereign government of such other nation.
Another matter which I think I should deal with at once is this, the idea mentioned by several speakers that the introduction of this bill at the present time had implications which went far beyond the declarations of policy enunciated by the Prime Minister on February 12, 1947. The purpose of this bill is to implement a portion of the declaration made on February 12, 1947, and goes no farther than that; and these implications that have been discussed, these prospective dangers that have been conjured up, cannot be founded on this bill or on the declaration of policy of February 12, 1947. If hon. members choose to imagine other possible policies, other possible dangers, I do not contest their right to do so, but let them do so on their own responsibility. In the presentation of this bill or in the policy declared to this house nothing is to be found which can serve as a basis for such feared possible consequences.

He asked where the government obtained the authority to invite the uniformed men of another nation on to Canadian soil. I replied I did not know of any statutory authority, but I pointed out that I thought it was something which could be done, if no prohibition was established by parliament against it.
During a discussion of the estimates in 1938 the then leader of the opposition, now Viscount Bennett, was criticizing something that had been discussed in the press about the establishment of training camps in this country by the government of the United Kingdom. I wish to say at once that it is quite inaccurate to say that there ever was any request and refusal. The situation was that the then leader of the opposition said, because of the known attitude of the government, "Of course there will be no request"; and that is where it ended.
I have before me Hansard for 1938, and I find at page 4523 a report of the discussion which took place when the estimates were before committee of the whole. Mr. Bennett said:	.

And then, to skip a few lines-
I believe other parts of the British empire have been considered, and the information is that not a request but what is equivalent to it, namely an approach to this government, was made to ascertain whether or not there would be any objection to this being done. Obviously no member of the commonwealth is going to ask this government, and face a refusal, because that is not the way governments do business.
Then, in dealing with that matter the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 4529 of Hansard for that year:
This government has never at any time said that it was not prepared to give in our own establishments the opportunity to British pilots to come over here and train, but they will do it in our own establishments, controlled by our own Minister of National Defence who is responsible to this parliament. That is an entirely different thing from having a branch of the British forces establish headquarters in this country, direct their own men here and be responsible, not to this parliament for what takes place in Canada as a consequence, but only to the British parliament and the British people.
That is exactly the situation; and I invite hon. members to compare that situation with the one described by the Prime Minister in his statement to the house on February 12 last, when he said:
As an underlying principle of all cooperative arrangements will be without impairment of the control of either country over all activities in its territory.
That is the arrangement as it exists at the present time, and for the properly carrying it out it is felt by the government that a bill of this kind is appropriate and even necessary. I think most hon. members who have had military experience have said that if there were to be groups of men of the forces of another country present in this country under the command of an officer or officers it would be proper and desirable that that officer or those officers should have the disciplinary powers provided for by this bill.

It was said in the debate, and rightly said, that matters	of	defence	policy	should be

We did nof think it would be proper to come to the house and say, "Pass an act under which *the governor in council can apply this legislation to any nation." The question *was asked: Well, what is the limit of this power of the governor in council to invite members of the armed, forces of a friendly nation to visit Canadian territory? The limit is the responsibility of the government to this house of parliament and to the country. The government is not as desirous of committing political suicide as was suggested in the course of the debate with respect to another matter last night. Any government, whether it be this one, or one formed of any other party, knows that for its acts it is responsible, first of all, to the opinion of the house and, then, to the opinion of the country. It is in the light of that responsibility that it carries out any policy over which it has these powers of management and control. With respect to the question as to why this matter was not put in the form of a treaty; well, hon. members have been very much concerned over the effect that even these joint statements might have in raising further suspicion in the minds of members of other governments. We do not overlook that. It does not bring us to the point where we refuse to recommend to parliament the appropriation of hundreds of millions of dollars for the preparation of defence. It does not deter us from doing the things that are recommended to us by those who are in charge of our general staff as being the prudent and proper things to do. But it 40es make us cautious; it does cause us to try to avoid doing anything unnecessary or anything which might be treated as alarming. We felt that if a treaty were made it would be seized upon as evidence supporting the impression that exists-I will not say how it is created-* as to the wide gulf between the two ideologies of the east and the western democracies, and as evidence that the countries of the western democracies are lining up, ganging up, against the rest of the world. And it was quite unnecessary. What was contemplated was merely the continuation of a policy that had been in operation for a number of years, and it was so stated by the Prime Minister in his declaration. If hon. members will read that declaration they will find that the Prime Minister was at pains to point out that since August, 1940, when the creation of the joint board on permanent defence was announced, it was stated by the President of the United States that the board-
. . . shall commence immediate studies relating to sea, land and air problems including personnel and material. It will consider in the broad sense the defence of the north half of the western hemisphere.
That was a year and a half before the United States became a belligerent in the last terrible war. The Prime Minister then declared that even the 1940 statement was merely a logical development of what had preceded it, and described in what manner that policy had been carried out in this country. Further, he went on to say that there was no treaty, no binding undertaking to continue; that it was a matter of cooperation along
parallel lines, to which both parties would conform so long as it suited them to do so, but to which neither party was bound for any time beyond that during which it suited its policies to do so. The declaration further stated that the decision was made-
... as a contribution to the stability of the world and to the establishment through the united nations of an effective system of worldwide security. With this in mind each government has sent a copy of this statement to the secretary general of the united nations for circulation to all its members.
Some of the debate in this house has almost implied that the adoption of this bill would be an alternative to Canada's participation in the united nations; and some of the debate would set up, on the one side, the hoped-for advantages to be derived from the united nations and, on the other, those to be derived from this kind of cooperation between Canada and her neighbour to the south. Well, it seems to me that is giving the Canadian public an entirely false impression. The corner-stone of Canada's policy, the corner-stone of the policy of our neighbour to the south, is the strength and validity and efficiency of the united nations organization; and that will ever continue to be the corner-stone of their policies. In spite of the many disappointments all of us have felt about the progress toward an efficient organization as contemplated by the charter of the united nations, I am still hopeful, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said, that the common sense of mankind all over the world will finally prevail and will allow us all to make the united nations organization an efficient working instrument for world peace and world security. But until we have a further demonstration of its ability to protect each one of us, then each one of us has to do his share to meet the conditions of a troubled world as they still exist; and that is the only justification for asking this parliament this year to appropriate 8226,000,000 for our national defence.
Another question was, how long will this act operate? I think this act, if it is passed in its present form, will operate for a long time. I think it will operate as long as a government supported by this party is in power, and that is too indefinite a period to attempt to place any limit upon it. But it can operate only when there are forces of a friendly nation on Canadian soil. If it should ever happen that hon. members opposite, either the group nearest Mr. Speaker or a group further removed, were in control of the government of Canada, it would be they who would decide whether or not forces of a

speechtext: The statute to which reference is made was that cited by me the night before last. It is public law 384 of the 78th congress, being chapter 326 of the second session of 1944. When the word ''co-belligerent" is used in the preamble it is used merely to describe the United Kingdom and Canada. Certainly my view is that even if the war ends legally, as no doubt it will at some future date, the fact that this word "co-belligerent" appears in the preamble would not cause the proclamation to cease to have effect, but that the law would continue to apply to forces of the United Kingdom and Canada until the contrary was proclaimed by the President.

Under section 2 (e) there is this provision:
"United States force" means any body, contingent or detachment of the military, naval or air forces of the United States of America that with the consent of the government of Canada, is lawfully present in Canada or on board any of His Majesty's Canadian ships or aircraft.
To deal particularly with the words "with the consent of the government of Canada," it seems clear from the explanations given thus far that, in practice, consent is given in this way, that the general staff decide what troops are invited to come to Canada, although the Prime Minister did say that the decisions of the department are reported by the minister. He was very indefinite about it. He more or less left the suggestion that the cabinet would hear about it.
I submit to the committee that this question of the giving of consent to for'eign troops to come to Canada is a matter about which there should be no uncertainty. We should have legislation providing for the way in which consent is to be given and under what conditions it is to be given. It is entirely too slipshod to leave it to the general staff. In my own opinion, it should not even be left to the cabinet without parliamentary sanction. There should be broad-based legislation by parliament for the giving of this consent, and I urge upon the government most strongly that they give consideration to bringing in legislation defining under just what conditions consent is to be given and how it is to be given. I think the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament are entitled to have some such provision written into our laws. There can be no objection to that from friendly foreign countries, and we would then know exactly where we were going and what to expect. I realize, of course, that this is a new situation but there will always be new

situations cropping up that have to be met by legislation. This is, I think, a typical example of a problem that has arisen which should be met by some definite legislation. speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver South no doubt in good faith referred to the terms on which United States officers or men may come to Canada as described by the' Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs earlier today in a way which I think Hansard will not support. The situation was fairly stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the Prime Minister. The situation is not as the hon. member for Vancouver South would have us believe. The general staff has full control over who will be invited and who will not. The situation is as described by the Prime Minister; that is, the policy is decided upon by the cabinet on a report from the Minister of National Defence or the defence committee of the cabinet. Then that policy is implemented within the power delegated to him by the appropriate minister and the appropriate military authority.
The major project on which there are Canadian officers and men associated with United States officers and men, and vice versa, working together in Canada is the project to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has just referred, namely the testing establishment at Churchill. That was specifically authorized by the cabinet, and the various changes in the possible size of the forces that might be there-and they are very small, as the minister has said-have come before the cabinet. But the cabinet does not say, we shall have three captains and two lieutenants and their name shall be John Brown, et cetera. That kind of arrangement and the carrying out of details, are done by the appropriate military officers. I can tell the committee that in the case of every other project so far undertaken in cooperation with the United States, either in the United States or in Canada, there has been full cabinet approval in advance. Then, when that approval has been given it is for the appropriate military,
naval or air authorities, within the terms delegated to them, to carry them out. It could not work in any other way.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Paragraph (e) says:
"United States force" means any body, contingent or detachment of the military, naval or air forces of the United States of America that, with the consent of the government of Canada, is lawfully present in Canada or on board any of His Majesty's Canadian ships or aircraft.
To my knowledge, we have had that on the great lakes since 1925. We recently had a great disaster on the upper lakes where a large number of sailors lost their lives. We have had these disasters take place in the chairman's constituency, and others in the constituencies of the maritimes. It has happened on lake Huron, the Georgian bay and on lake Superior. subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA

something which might give rise to an attempt to restrain, its application. We said, "What we are concerned about is that we want to be sure that you are not going to apply any of your laws to anyone who, according to the decisions of our courts, would not be amenable to your laws."

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Then I should like to know also in what manner there is Canadian control over United States troops. That, I think, comes under this section. It was for the purpose of asking this question that I quoted from the Prime Minister's statemnt of July 1, 1938, which upset the Secretary of State for External Affairs so much only a few minutes ago. The Prime Minister then said that British pilots coming to Canada would train in our own establishments, controlled by our own Minister of National Defence, who is responsible to this parliament. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said this afternoon that United States troops coming here would really come only for training.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
No.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I explained that if training were to cover everything covered in the statement, that would be right. But what is covered in the statement is described in language which may not be mere training; it is not the word "training" which is used. It may be covered by what the hon. member has in mind when he uses the word "training". But this testing of materials is not really the training of individuals. I would understand that "training" would be something to increase the military skill or prowess of the individual so trained. But that is not what is being done.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
In my questions this afternoon I distinguished between "training" and "establishing posts". I asked the minister whether the Americans would be establishing posts here, and I understood him to say-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not under the present arrangement.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
-that what they were going to do would come rather under the heading of "training."
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
That, of course, brings
them under the Prime Minister's statement of July 1, 1938, which was that British pilots would have to train under our own establishments, controlled by our own Minister of National Defence. I understand, further, that the arrangements with the Americans are to be similar. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
If so, in what manner is
the Department of National Defence to control these United States forces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
In exactly the same way as control is exercised in respect of Canadian forces. That is not through power of command ; that comes down through another chain, but through the direction regarding the operation of any testing establishment, or things of such nature as may be set up. All those will be Canadian.
First of all, the man in charge will be a Canadian, under this arrangement as announced by the Prime Minister on February 12. The man in charge of each establishment will be Canadian. Instructions given to him will be given pursuant to policy which I as Minister of National Defence, interpret from the cabinet to the military authorities.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
How are we to work out
these provisions whereby they shall be trained in our own establishments?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They are our establishments. They are establishments under our flag. The man at the head of the establishment, and responsible to us for everything that occurs in the establishment, is a Canadian officer.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: I think it is really a. question of a technical nature which the Minister of National Defence should answer, the question as to how they are being trained in our establishments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: I do not see the hon. member's difficulty at all.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Obviously the intention in 1938 was that they would come into Canadian establishments. Is that the intention with regard to the United States troops; and, if so, how is that to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: In exactly the same way as if they were Canadian troops coming in for the purpose, of course, that is the intention.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Section 3 states, in part, that the service courts and service authorities of the United States of America may exercise within Canada or on board any such ship or aircraft in relation to members of that force all such powers as are conferred upon them by the law of the United States of America. It seems to me that that provision has elements of uncertainty in it, owing to the fact that at the present time the law of the United States with respect to service courts and service personnel may be sufficiently similar to our own that, under certain conditions, the Minister of National Defence is prepared to
38S2
Visiting Forces

accept it. Supposing, however, that we pass this section and that, a year from now, the United States made a drastic change with respect to the powers of service courts for service personnel not envisaged at the present time.
It seems to me we have not here a safeguard to provide for the contingency of a law being passed by another foreign power which might be repugnant to ourselves. Is there any difficulty in that regard?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not see why we should be concerned, so long as we make sure that their law is applied only to members of their force, and that we do not leave it to them to say who are members of their force. If we say that no one in Canada shall be treated as a member of their force unless, if he objects, a Canadian court says, "You are a member of their force and you are subject to their law", it seems to me it is not really our concern to say, "Well, now, before you apply your law to a member of your force we would like to be satisfied that it is good law."

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Assuming there is a penalty for striking an officer and that a man is to be shot for it-and we will assume that as an extreme case-
Mr.* ST. LAURENT: I could not assume that as something ordered by the laws of our friends to the south.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: No, of course not. I cannot either. But we are not protecting ourselves in that regard.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: I should like a little bit of clarification as to exactly what these powers are. I ask these questions really because I have run into quite a bit of discussion around the corridors and in private conversation with members who were far from clear as to the exact meaning of this section and the next one. Perhaps the thing could be made clearer by example than in any other way. As I understand the matter, if a United States soldier goes absent without leave or deserts, in that case discipline is entirely in the hands of the United States army officer under whose command that man comes. We will say that the United States soldier is alleged to have murdered a Canadian citizen. In that case who has jurisdiction? In other words, where is the United States soldier to be tried? Is he to be tried in his own United States court or in one of our civil courts?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Under this law, it would be possible for him to be tried under his own military court, but that would not exclude the jurisdiction of our courts. Even if he
[.Mr. Probe.]
were tried and acquitted under the United States military court, he could still be tried, sentenced and the sentence carried out under the jurisdiction of our courts. This does not exclude in any way the operation of our courts; and in an offence as serious as suggested by the hon. member, there is no doubt that the man would be tried in our courts.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Would the same rule apply to an American who was accused of theft from a Canadian citizen, we will say?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Then, if a United States soldier is involved in an automobile accident and does damage to a Canadian citizen's car and person, where is the jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: He would still be civilly and criminally liable under our laws before the Canadian courts.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Suppose he is really breaking one of our highway rules. Is he to be prosecuted in our court and then subsequently be liable to a civil action by the Canadian citizen?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Absolutely.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Or is he to be dealt with in the United States court as far as the highway violation is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: No. The Canadian courts would have jurisdiction.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
In that case, it would be entire jurisdiction, would it?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If they choose to exercise it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: If the Canadian courts choose to exercise it, they would have jurisdiction. But. that would not prevent the United States service court from, in addition, exercising its jurisdiction if a military offence under military law had also been committed during the same set of circumstances.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Take the case of a crime which is entirely within one United States detachment. Suppose one United States soldier murders another one. Is that something that will be left entirely to the United States army court to deal with, or would our courts step into the picture?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Nothing takes away the jurisdiction of our courts.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
The presumption is that the case of this man would be left entirely in the hands of the United States military authorities.

Visiting Forces

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: I would doubt that. That would be a matter for the Minister of Justice at the time or the attorney general of the province to decide. He would have jurisdiction to say what should happen there. I would doubt if the attorney general of the province would leave it to the United States court.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: In that case it really comes down to the initiative or action of the attorney general of the province. He is free at any time, in any case, to step in if a Canadian law has been broken.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: The untrammelled jurisdiction of the Canadian courts is not in any way affected by this.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Jurisdiction of civil courts in Canada not affected.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I just wish to follow up what was being discussed a moment ago. Suppose an American commits an offence against the criminal code. Let us say it is a small offence, that he is arrested by his own detachment or by his own officers and tried. Could we then demand the custody of that person in order to try him in our own courts?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The jurisdiction of our courts has not been interfered with. It was explained to the United States authorities that, except under war conditions, the administration of justice was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial authorities, that we could give their service courts concurrent jurisdiction, but that we did not propose to interfere with the rights to exercise and discharge their responsibility which are held by those who had the responsibility for ordinary administration of justice.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
That is to say, if the soldier had been detained and tried by a United States service court, and then we wished to take action, we could go and demand to arrest that person?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Is there correspondence to that effect between the department and the United States authorities? Is there an understanding in correspondence between the authorities of the United States and ourselves that this can be done?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The correspondence we have had with them is to this effect: "Here, there are not going to be very many of you here; we do not think you are going to get 83166-248
into trouble very often, but when any of your people do get into trouble we think you will probably treat them in a manner that will satisfy the public opinion of the locality that adequate measures of restraint have been taken. But we will not abandon any jurisdiction of our own courts, and you must expect that if what you do makes the people where the offence takes place feel that our courts should deal with the matter, they will deal with it."

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, I understand that. I was just referring to the question of actual arrest, as to whether or not we are prevented from doing that if he is lawfully detained by the service court of the United States. I was referring to the actual arrest itself.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would not want to pronounce judgment on anything of that kind, but I think the hon. member will agree with me that, without an act, nothing the United States authorities would do would constitute lawful detention.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Oh, yes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. Nothing they would do, unless they have authority from the Canadian law to do it, would constitute lawful detention. Here we give them authority, but we say, "Nothing in the authority we give you is going to interfere with the rights of our own people to administer Canadian justice." I think that is as clear as I can make it.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
It seems to me that we may be running into a legal difficulty here as far as our own service courts are concerned. Any civil-and I use "civil" as opposed to "military"-offence comes under the civil court if there is a competent court of civil jurisdiction in the area. Apparently all our own troops would be tried in civil courts; all troops that were visiting here from Great Britain, Australia, India or anywhere else in the British empire would be tried in our civil courts; but United States troops would be tried in their own courts for what are really civil offences such as theft, murder and so forth. That may result in this situation. A man may be tried in a United States court and perhaps acquitted. But the attorney general of the province lays a charge against him. He is brought up in a civil court. Under our law, as I have always understood it, and particularly as far as the military end of things is concerned in the army act, that man having been tried and acquitted in the United States court, cannot be tried again under our law. In other words, he cannot be tried the second

Visiting Forces

time. I would think we are likely to run into difficulties in that way. What would be the situation? What is the answer to that?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Section 4 declares
that nothing they are authorized to do will interfere with the ordinary administration by our courts and our officials of our laws, for offences against our laws. We have declared, however, that if we deal with them under our laws for offences against our laws and acquit them, that acquittal will prevail in their service courts; but the reverse is not true.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
That comes into conflict, though, with the general principle in our law that a man may be tried only once for an offence.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Do you think it is a good thing to have that exception to the general rule under our law?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think it is. I believe it is necessary for us in Canada to say, "No matter what you do, if one of your people commits an offence against Canadian law, Canadian authorities must have it within their power, if they see fit to do so, to deal with it as they would deal with a Canadian resident." That is particularly true in our country where the administration of justice is the responsibility of the provinces. During the war we could say, "Well, because of the emergency we can override some provisions of provincial jurisdiction"; but during normal times we do not want to attempt to do that. During normal times we think the attorney general of a province, who is responsible to his people for the administration of law and order in that province, should not be restricted by any arrangement we make with the Americans in respect of their forces. So we say to them, "If having done that, we acquit one of your men, you must not try to prosecute him again. But if you acquit a man before we deal with him, in one of your service courts, of course that is no business of ours. We have to deal with him just as if nothing had been done".

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
It seems to me that a great many of the complexities and jurisdictional disputes which conceivably could take place under this legislation could have been avoided. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that these United States troops are few in number and are doing simple business such as the testing of materials, and so on. I believe United States civilians could have
come here to perform those duties, without having to wear United States uniforms. They could have carried out those scientific experiments, which apparently is what they are, and as civilians would have been amenable to all Canadian laws without any of these difficulties. What was wrong with that? Or why was not the general practice adopted in the treatment of troops in another country in peace time, under which practice they were first tried in civil courts and then taken to the border and turned over, as extradited criminals might be, to be dealt with by their own governments in their own lands and punished by whatever procedure might be considered fit? Why could that not be done in peace time? That is what is done with a criminal who commits offences in two countries. He is punished first in one place and then turned over to the authorities in the other country. Why could there not be a similar arrangement here?

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I presume that this section is to cover the case of a United States soldier who has been found guilty by his own service court and is being held in detention and there would be no writ of habeas corpus in our courts. I can envision the case of a United States soldier who may be found guilty of a breach of a regulation which would not constitute a crime in Canada, and then escapes. Under our criminal code anyone who has been sentenced by a court of competent jurisdiction and who is at large in Canada while under term of imprisonment, commits a criminal offence. If a soldier escapes like that would we be bound to help to arrest him where the crime committed is not a crime recognized in Canada?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think the hon. member will find the answer to his question in section 7 which reads:
7. For the purpose of enabling the service courts and service authorities of the United States of America to exercise more effectively the powers conferred upon them by this act, the Minister of National Defence, if so requested by the officer commanding a United States force or by the government of the United States of America, may from time to time by general or special orders to any home force direct the members thereof to arrest members of the United States force alleged to have been guilty of offences against the law of the United States of America and to hand over any person so arrested to the appropriate authorities of the United States force.
I take it that that is the procedure which would be followed. If they wish to have the assistance of the Canadian authorities they
would apply, either through the state department or through the United States officer, to the Canadian government or to the Minister of National Defence and he would, if he saw fit, and should, I suppose, if it were a proper case, give an order to render the assistance necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 7 agreed to.
On section 8-Temporary detention.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Subsection 1 of this section reads:
Any member of a United States force, if sentenced iby a service court of the United States of America to penal servitude, imprisonment or detention may, under the authority of the Minister of National Defence, given at the request of the officer commanding the United States force, be temporarily detained in custody in a detention barrack in Canada.
Will the minister state whether that will be done at the expense of Canada, or whether expenses in connection with detention will be recoverable from the United States government?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It would be anticipated that any expense to which Canada was put on behalf of officers of the United States forces would be reimbursed to the Canadian authorities.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Is it contemplated that the United States will have detention barracks in this country?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That matter has not been gone into and I do not think it would be practicable to express any views upon it. There are only a small number of these men here and there has been no occasion to consider whether or not they should have detention barracks of their own. I would say that there would be no insuperable objection if there were two or three hundred at a place where their military police had a room in which could be temporarily detained members of their forces who had been apprehended. So far the matter has not come up as a practical proposition.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Is the United States government acquiring installations, buildings and so on as they did during war time?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; it is understood that they are not to acquire any permanent property. To be quite frank, so far they have been paying us rental for barracks or huts, and there is on foot a project under which they will contribute to the erection of other bar-
83166- 248i
Visiting Forces

racks and pay in advance for a stated period what would be the equivalent of the rental to His Majesty in the right of Canada.

On section 9-Certain provisions of criminal code not applicable.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister whether there is a reciprocal arrangement with the United States. When we were discussing this matter this afternoon it was contended that we have the same rights in the United States as their forces have here. Is there a similar arrangement whereby Canadian troops are exempt from similar provisions of their criminal law as United States troops are to be exempted from the sections of the criminal code set out in this section?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: We are told that that is so in fact. As the hon. member knows, criminal laws in the United States are state laws; they are not something that can be dealt with by the central government. We are told that the proper application of the doctrine accepted by Chief Justice Marshall would be such as to prevent the application of state laws to the parading with arms of members of the forces of a friendly power who were in the country with the consent of the central government.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Section 9(1) provides that certain sections of the criminal code shall not apply to a member of a United States force in Canada acting in the course of his duty, and specifically section 99 of the code is referred to respecting military exercises, movements or evolutions. This provision is not quite on all fours with what the minster said earlier in the day, that the number of troops and their present duties in this country are of such a nature that they are simply testing equipment. It would, therefore, suggest itself to me that there cannot, under the present arrangements, be military movements or exercises of a type that might be construed as drilling. Does the minister foresee such conditions occurring in the future? Is that the reason section 99 of the criminal code is not made applicable to the United States troops, or is this just a general precaution?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not think the numbers I have mentioned would preclude drilling. I remember that a good many years ago when I was a lad there was a company of cavalry in my village and I would be surprised if they numbered more than forty, but they took pretty seriously the drilling to which they subjected themselves and their

horses. We used to look upon it as pretty efficient drilling. There will certainly be a sufficient number at the Churchill establishment to make it possible for them to have a parade and to go through movements that would, I think, come within the description of drilling.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-Coming into force.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I would ask whether a similar bill has been passed by the United States congress?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, a bill was passed by the congress of the United States in 1944. It is not fully similar to this, because all they had to do there was to make provision by legislation to impose duties upon their own citizens. Their construction of international law as determined by their supreme court was	such that	they	did not	find itnecessary to adopt a statute to recognize the jurisdiction of officers	over	men under theircommand	present in	the	territory	of theUnited States, but they did have to have legislation	to impose	upon citizens	of the
United States the duty of rendering assistance to enable officers to exercise in a practical way the jurisdiction they had by international law.
I must make a further qualification. I do not know that there was any provision in the United States statute that it should apply as from a specific date. The reason for making this legislation apply as from the first day of April, 1947, is that we told our friends representing the United States authority that we would get this legislation through at an early day. They felt a bit uneasy since the time the orders in council were repealed, and we said: "If you have done anything in the meantime we will ask parliament to declare that this statute shall be deemed to have come into force on the first day of April, so that there will be no hiatus in your jurisdiction.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the accession of Canada to the convention on the privileges and immunities of the united nations and to grant to the united nations and any specialized agency of which Canada is a member and which is brought into relationship with the united nations, to their officers and to the representatives of their members, the

subtopic: ACCESSION OP CANADA TO CONVENTION ON PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES
speechtext:
This is a rather large order. The minister tabled a list of the countries, numbering some twenty-eight, which have agencies here in Ottawa, and ambassadors. You will have to build a new hotel or several houses for them, because they will take up about one-third of the accommodation. A list of the countries which have these privileges and immunities was given to us some time ago. Another list of Canada's expeditionary force, known as ambassadors overseas, has been tabled. It will be found that we have ambassadors in almost every country on the seven seas. The expenses of the department are going up; they are $1,700,000 more than they were last year. When you add that to the $1,500,000 for trade commissioners in the same places it amounts to $3,200,000 extra this year. The report that the minister brought down covers nearly twenty-five pages. It gives a list of the non-commissioned officers and men, the first secretaries, the second secretaries, the third secretaries and, all kinds of officials.
I have never been to a meeting of the united nations. I have not much confidence in the whole organization because of what happened at San Francisco and Lake Success. Before they get through, we shall have to call it Lake Failure, but it is nothing but a talking tower of babel.
Look at the people to whom this resolution applies. I am surprised to find the list. Talk about the noble four hundred. I venture to say that if the list is counted the number will come to pretty nearly four hundred; it will reach to several centuries.
The minister says that it is expedient to introduce a measure. I doubt at this time, with all the talk there is going on, whether it is expedient to know more about the organization to which we are granting the rights and privileges for which the ordinary taxpayer will have to pay. The resolution says that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the accession of Canada to the convention on the privileges and immunities of the united nations. There are a lot of these conventions; we are getting them all mixed up. There was a Liberal convention some time ago. I do not know whether they could qualify here or whether they should qualify. They ought to have certain rights and immunities, Mr. Chairman, as well as these other gentlemen who belong to these other countries and
United, Nations

organizations. My hon. friends to the left have a convention sometimes, and my hon. friends farther down the aisle-

I know the minister is a hard working man, but the people are becoming very much alarmed at the united nations. Mr. Attlee himself complained the other day and said he was very much disappointed in it the first year. I think he is right.
The resolution goes on to describe other specialized agencies of which Canada is a member, which are "brought into relationship with the united nations, to their officers and to their representatives of their members, the legal capacity" and so forth. Every one of these gentlemen will have an adviser, a legal officer. Why do they belong to the organization if they must have somebody to advise them? There is the first officer, the second officer, the third officer, and all that kind of thing. The resolution continues and mentions the "legal capacity, immunities, facilities and privileges necessary for the accomplishment of the purposes of the united nations and of its specialized agencies." I fail to see why we should have a class like this. We are giving all these officers of the countries which belong to the united nations the rights and privileges of ambassador's and are exempting them from taxation. Many other advantages are given to them. It is becoming privilege and nothing but privilege. Some have relief and some have not.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would hope that hon. members would prefer to have the discussion on this matter after they got the bill. The charter of the united nations provides that that organization and its affiliated agencies will enjoy such immunities as are necessary for them to accomplish the purpose for which they are established. Article 105 of the charter to which the houses of the Canadian parliament have acceded, says:
The general assembly may make recommendations with a view to determining the details of the applications of paragraphs 1 and 2 of this article or may propose conventions to the members of the united nations for this purpose.
The conventions proposed are not gatherings of members of a party; they are agreements setting out what the privileges and immunities are to be. I am sure it will be the wish of all members that the Canadian parliament give consideration to the matter. The conven-

tion has been prepared. All that this resolution does is to ask leave to introduce a bill to which the convention is annexed, so that the members may give it consideration. There are already a large number of states that have given their adherence to this convention, and I think it would be preferable to reserve the debate that we shall have on the propriety of acceding to the convention to the time when the bill is introduced and the convention placed before members of parliament, and they are in a position to discuss it in an appropriate manner.
All that we are asking at the present time is that we have leave to introduce a bill to which the convention will be attached, so that members of parliament can consider it and decide whether or not they want Canada to accept it as other members of the united nations have done.

The various specialized agencies, established by intergovernmental agreement and having wide international responsibilities, as defined in their basic instruments, in economic, social, cultural, educational, health, and related fields, shall be brought into relationship with the united nations in accordance with the provisions of article 63.

Our sales there are not at all sufficient to enable us to make payment for what we are purchasing, and the proceeds of our sales to countries which pay in sterling are not readily convertible either into gold or into United States dollars. It would seem to me to be a matter of great importance to know exactly the position of our foreign exchange reserves. That would be almost a determining factor in deciding whether or not these bonds should be retired, even though the interest would seem to be high at the present time. May I make a remark that may clear up something? I have given the bill a little study and it seems to me that we have been talking at crosspurposes. I think what the bill says is this. It really authorizes the treasury to lend money on notes to the Canadian National Railways. That is what section 7 says. In the earlier sections, provision is made for assigning substituted securities for the securities which are paid in by the $200 million or such portion of the $200 million as may be decided on, so that tonight all we are asked to do is to authorize the borrowings on notes. "Notes" is the word

used in section 7. In other words, the government gets a note from the Canadian National Railways for such portion of the $200 million as the railway wants to borrow from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY COMPANY MATURING OR CALLABLE BOND ISSUES, 1947-1954

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY COMPANY MATURING OR CALLABLE BOND ISSUES, 1947-1954

speechtext: Why would the government be guaranteeing, then?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY COMPANY MATURING OR CALLABLE BOND ISSUES, 1947-1954
speechtext:
I am coming to that. Against that borrowing we then have

Canadian National Railways
securities issued by the railway which the government guarantees and, according to section 4, these securities may be mostly in kind or issued probably at any time the government chooses. I hope the parliamentary assistant to the minister will agree that I have now perhaps-I hope finally-found out just what the gist of the bill is. Therefore all that we are really doing tonight is authorizing a loan from the treasury up to the S200 million to the Canadian National Railways on notes. Then we also authorize the treasury to guarantee new securities in substitution for those which are brought in and cremated as is provided in the act. So far as I am concerned I have some confusion in mind. I thought the securities were to be sold immediately or something of that sort in order to take up this $200 million. That is not so. The $200 million is a loan on a note as it is used. Then the government guarantees the securities issued by the railway company to take up the reclaimed outstanding bonds, or whatever they are. Having regard to our exchange situation- and this may be an amateurish suggestion- would it not be worth while considering the issue of new securities payable in New York in United States dollars at a discount, and thus, for the present at least, avoid paying bonuses-of ten per cent, as it is at the present time-in New York to get the United States dollars to pay off our present securities? That may not be a good suggestion, but it is one which has occurred to me.

speechtext: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved the second reading of Bill No. 205, to amend the War Charities Act, 1939.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENT CONFINING PROVISIONS OF ACT TO FUNDS ALREADY REGISTERED
speechtext:
The house is travelling a little behind schedule tonight, and I appreciate that the government may wish to have the bill disposed of in the few remaining minutes, if possible.
In the first place, I draw attention to the fact that this bill is an inevitable kind of bill, because the position of charities must revert at some time or another to the situation which existed prior to the war. The purpose of the bill is, therefore, such that it deserves the support of the house in so far as it seeks to close the class of charities to which the War Charities Act applies and which must submit to registration in accordance with the act before they are entitled to seek moneys by way of subscription.
The explanatory note I suggest, Mr. Speaker, overstates the effect of the bill. The bill provides that the application of the act shall be confined to war charities established prior to the coming into force of the act. Of course there is a difference between establishing the fund and submitting it to registration, and the explanatory note says that the effect of the amendment is, therefore, to confine the provision of the act to funds already registered for the purpose of complete administration of such funds and to free from the provisions of the act any new funds which would otherwise 83166-249J
require to be registered. As the bill stands, of course it cannot have that effect because the effect of the bill as it now reads is to limit the effect of the act to charities established, whether registered or not, prior to the coming into force of the act. If the intention is as stated in the explanatory note, then I suggest that the bill will have to be amended when the house goes into committee. It may be that there are some new charities which are within the scope of the act but are not yet registered, since the 1945 amendment extended the scope of the War Charities Act to include funds to be used for the purpose of providing war memorials. Perhaps the minister can deal with that when he speaks.
There is one other matter-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENT CONFINING PROVISIONS OF ACT TO FUNDS ALREADY REGISTERED
speechtext: So that we may save time, the provision is intended to apply to anything that is not already a registered charity, war memorial or otherwise.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENT CONFINING PROVISIONS OF ACT TO FUNDS ALREADY REGISTERED
speechtext:
Then I suggest to the minister that when we get into committee the word '"established" should be amended to read "registered", and that will clarify it.
There is one matter that, I think, does call for some explanation. Section 12 of the Department of National War Services Act requires that an annual report be submitted to parliament, but the last report issued by this department covering the administration of war charities is the report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1945. The administration of this act was transferred from the Minister of National War Services to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by P.C. 134, dated January 14, of this year. That does not' I submit, override the requirement of the act in connection with annual reports to parliament. A report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946, should have been submitted long ago, and none has yet been submitted.
